p.src: It happened in the summer three years ago. Like any ordinary traveler, I shouldered a rucksack and set out from that hot-spring inn in Kamikochi to climb Mount Hotaka. As you know, the only way to climb Mount Hotaka is to follow the Azusa River upstream. Since I had climbed not only Mount Hotaka but Mount Yari as well, I proceeded without a guide up the valley of the Azusa River, over which the morning mist had descended. Up the valley of the Azusa River beneath the morning mist—yet no matter how long I waited, the mist showed no sign of lifting. On the contrary, it only grew thicker. After walking for about an hour, I began to wonder whether I ought to turn back to the hot-spring inn at Kamikochi. But even if I were to turn back to Kamikochi, I would first have to wait for the mist to clear. And yet, with every passing moment, the mist merely thickened and thickened. “Oh, what the devil—I may as well keep climbing.” —Having made up my mind, I pushed my way through the dwarf bamboo, taking care not to stray from the Azusa River valley. But all that met my eyes was still the dense mist. To be sure, now and then I could make out through the mist the thick trunks of Japanese beeches and the branches of firs, their lush green leaves hanging down. Grazing horses and cattle, too, would suddenly thrust their faces into view before me. But the instant I caught sight of them, they vanished again into the billowing mist. Before long my legs grew weary and my stomach began to complain—and, to make matters worse, my climbing clothes and blankets, soaked through by the mist, had become extraordinarily heavy. At last I gave in and decided to descend into the Azusa River valley, guided by the sound of water rushing between the rocks. I sat down on a rock at the water’s edge and, for the moment, set about having my meal.

But all that met my eyes was still the dense mist.

I sat down on a rock at the water’s edge and, for the moment, set about having my meal.

p.src: I opened a tin of corned beef, gathered dead branches, and lit a fire—and while I was busy with such things, some ten minutes must have passed. Meanwhile, the relentlessly spiteful mist had somehow begun faintly to clear. Nibbling at my bread, I glanced down at my wristwatch. It was already twenty minutes past one. But what startled me more was the sudden shadow of a strange, sinister face falling across the round glass of my watch. Startled, I turned around. And there—this was, in fact, the very first time I had ever seen a kappa. On a rock behind me stood a kappa exactly like the ones in pictures, one arm wrapped around the trunk of a white birch and the other hand held above its eyes, gazing down at me with evident curiosity.

ja: いちじにじゅうふんす
u.src: It was already twenty minutes past one.
But what startled me more was the sudden shadow of a strange, sinister face falling across the round glass of my watch.
Startled, I turned around.
And there—this was, in fact, the very first time I had ever seen a kappa.

On a rock behind me stood a kappa exactly like the ones in pictures, one arm wrapped around the trunk of a white birch and the other hand held above its eyes, gazing down at me with evident curiosity.

p.src: I was so taken aback that for a while I stood there without moving. The kappa, too, appeared startled and did not even move the hand held above its eyes. Presently, no sooner had I sprung up than I leapt at the kappa on the rock. At the same instant, the kappa also fled. Or rather, I suppose it fled. The truth is, the moment I thought it had nimbly dodged aside, it vanished somewhere in a flash. More astonished than ever, I looked around among the dwarf bamboo. Then I saw the kappa two or three metres away, still poised to flee, looking back at me. There was nothing strange about that. What did surprise me, however, was the colour of the kappa's body. The kappa that had watched me from the rock had been grey all over. But now its entire body had turned completely green. “Damn you!” I cried at the top of my voice and leapt at the kappa once more. Naturally, the kappa ran away. For the next half hour or so, I charged through the dwarf bamboo, vaulted over rocks, and pursued the kappa with reckless determination. The kappa was so fleet-footed that it was certainly no slower than a monkey. As I chased it in a frenzy, I nearly lost sight of it time and again. What was more, I often slipped and went tumbling. But when we came beneath a great horse-chestnut tree whose thick branches spread wide, fortunately a grazing cow stood directly in the kappa's path. And it was a bull with thick horns and bloodshot eyes. At the sight of the bull, the kappa let out some sort of shriek and pitched headlong into an especially tall patch of dwarf bamboo. I—thinking, “Now I've got you!”—immediately rushed after it. There must have been some hole there that I knew nothing about.

p.src: Just as my fingertips finally brushed the kappa's slippery back, I suddenly plunged headfirst into profound darkness. Yet even at such a hairbreadth moment of peril, the human mind is capable of thinking the most preposterous things. At the very instant I thought, “Ah!” I remembered that beside the hot-spring inn at Kamikochi there was a bridge called Kappa Bridge. After that—after that, I remember nothing. I merely sensed something like a flash of lightning before my eyes, and before I knew it, I had lost consciousness.
